Lead story

Ray: Okay, so here's the problem. If you want to predict the temperature where a magnet orders, you need two things. Accurate exchange interactions, which are how neighboring spins push on each other, and a proper treatment of the spin thermodynamics.

Ada: And the cheap way to do the thermodynamics is classical Monte Carlo, where spins are treated as little arrows, not quantum objects.

Ray: Right. And the paper tests a previously proposed fix. Rescale the classical temperatures by a factor of S plus one, over S, where S is the spin.

Ray: They checked it directly. They took seventeen compounds, used Heisenberg models built from inelastic neutron scattering data, and compared classical Monte Carlo against quantum stochastic series expansion simulations.

Ada: Hold on. What's the reference there? Is that experiment?

Ray: Good catch. No. The quantum simulations of the same model are the benchmark. The neutron data sets up the model's exchange couplings, but the comparison is classical versus quantum on that one model.

Ray: The result: the mean absolute temperature difference drops from eighty one point seven kelvin to eight point two kelvin. That's a mean absolute percentage difference of five point nine percent.

Ada: That's a big improvement. But does it work for real metals?

Ray: The paper says the benchmark holds within the tested models. The summary points out those are mostly insulating systems, and it doesn't say anything about metals.

Ada: There was also a second part, right? Diffusion Monte Carlo.

Ray: Yes. For five insulating antiferromagnets, they compared diffusion Monte Carlo and density functional theory against references rebuilt from neutron exchanges. Diffusion Monte Carlo underestimates those references, but its mean absolute error is comparable to the best functionals tested.

Ada: So it isn't a clear winner.

Ray: Not in this test. The takeaway is that better electronic energies alone won't do it. You also have to pay attention to quantum spin thermodynamics.

Magnets and materials

Ray: On to our magnets and materials desk. First, a data story. UniHam is a dataset of over one hundred thousand density functional theory Hamiltonians, covering seventy two elements, and all of them include full spin orbit coupling.

Ada: And spin orbit coupling matters because it controls magnetic anisotropy, a magnet's preference for certain crystal directions.

Ray: Yes. They benchmark two models on reconstruction, out of distribution generalization, and downstream property prediction.

Ray: The summary doesn't say either way.

Ray: Next, paired dopants in the layered semiconductors molybdenum diselenide and tungsten diselenide. Using DFT plus U calculations, the researchers found that pairs of dopants are more stable than isolated ones.

Ray: They report in-plane anisotropy energy up to minus three point five millielectron volts, and a Monte Carlo Curie temperature near four hundred forty kelvin for a two iron dopant in molybdenum diselenide.

Ada: And that minus sign just means the magnetization prefers lying in the plane. Also, that's a calculation, not a sample someone measured.

Ray: Correct. It's all computed.

Ray: Last one. A study asking whether a graph neural network's feature rankings reflect real physics. On cobalt molybdenum iron nickel copper alloys, they swapped individual atoms and re-ranked features. The influence decayed with distance, consistent with the network's interaction cutoff.

Ada: Nice template for auditing explanations. Small dataset, though, and not magnetism.

Metal printing

Ray: Over to metal printing. A paper on laser powder bed fusion uses a policy gradient reinforcement learning controller to hold surface temperature steady. It combines feedback inside each layer with feedforward control between layers.

Ada: Simulation, or a real printer?

Ray: Both. The physical test used a simplified, hardware constrained version, tuned offline from one uncontrolled calibration layer. It cut mean tracking error by three point four percent and input constraint violations by forty seven point five percent, against a Bayesian optimization baseline.

Ada: Three point four percent is modest.

Ray: It is. The paper frames it as matching state of the art. It also reports a new class of high frequency excitation that reduced vector head swelling.

Ray: Next, GreenMelt, a fast melt pool model with latent heat and Marangoni flow, which is surface tension driven motion of the liquid metal. It computes single track melt pool temperatures in one to ten seconds on a laptop, versus three and a half to five and a half hours for computational fluid dynamics.

Ada: And accuracy?

Ray: Average relative error in the mushy zone is below three percent. But that's validated on single tracks, so part scale agreement is still to be shown.

Ray: Third, Fed-PIGANO. Several sites train a shared physics informed neural operator without sharing their part geometries. Across twelve scenario and site cases, relative error was one point eight three to two point zero four percent, versus up to twenty point four six percent for local only training.

Ada: Real parts?

Ray: No, a two dimensional steady state thermal benchmark. A surrogate model result, not live sensing.

Quantum benchmark tests (S+1)/S rescaling of classical MC temperatures

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 7/10

Classical Monte Carlo simulations of magnets can be checked against quantum benchmarks. The abstract reports that rescaling classical temperatures by a spin-dependent factor, (S+1)/S, cuts the mean classical-quantum difference across 17 compounds from 81.7 K to 8.2 K, using Heisenberg models derived from inelastic neutron scattering. It also reports that a quantum Monte Carlo method (DMC) underestimates exchange energy differences in five antiferromagnets, which matters because the tested models are mostly insulating systems rather than metals.

Cycle-space Wang-Landau gives partition functions at all temperatures at once

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 7/10

The abstract describes a sampling method that walks over the null space of a lattice's incidence matrix. Because its weight distribution does not depend on temperature, a single run yields thermodynamics at any temperature rather than requiring separate simulations for each. It is checked against exact triangular-lattice Ising results and applied to 3D and 4D Ising and Baxter-Wu models, but the abstract shows no real-material demonstration.

UniHam: 100k+ DFT Hamiltonians with full spin-orbit coupling

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports a dataset of over 100,000 complex Hermitian Hamiltonians including spin-orbit coupling, covering 72 elements, along with benchmarks of two models on reconstruction, out-of-distribution generalization and downstream properties. Spin-orbit coupling controls magnetocrystalline anisotropy, the preference of a magnet for particular crystal directions, so a dataset like this could help train models that predict it. The summary does not make clear whether the downstream tasks include magnetic properties or how well cerium's f-electrons are covered.

Zigzag ladder with anisotropic Γ term: only gapped phases, TLL only when isotropic

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The paper revisits the phase diagram of a spin-1/2 Heisenberg zigzag ladder with an anisotropic Γ term, a model tied to the mineral YbCuS2, using exact diagonalization, DMRG and effective theories. It reports Néel, dimer, ferromagnetic and double-Néel phases, all gapped, with Gaussian c=1 transitions, and a Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid appears only when the coupling is isotropic. It is a one-dimensional quantum model, so it shows how anisotropic exchange reshapes phases but does not directly describe bulk three-dimensional magnets.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Paired dopants in MoSe2/WSe2 give large MAE and ~440 K Tc

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

Researchers studied pairs of transition-metal dopants in the semiconducting layered materials MoSe2 and WSe2 using DFT+U calculations. The abstract reports in-plane magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) up to -3.5 meV, and a Monte Carlo estimate of the Curie temperature near 440 K for a two-iron dopant in MoSe2. The negative sign means the magnetization prefers to lie in the plane rather than point out of it.

Neural quantum states for Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Heisenberg magnets

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

The authors use neural-network wavefunctions to find ground-state energies of chiral spin systems with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions in 2D and 3D. The abstract reports energies competitive with DMRG, a leading quantum method, and tighter upper bounds for periodic and layered geometries. It targets the lowest-energy quantum state rather than a transition temperature, so it does not give magnetic ordering temperatures directly.

Perturbation tests check whether GNN feature rankings are physical

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

For CoMoFeNiCu decomposition enthalpy, the authors test whether a graph neural network's feature rankings reflect real physics by swapping atoms and re-ranking the features. They find that the influence decays with distance in a way consistent with the network's interaction cutoff. The check is a useful template for auditing machine-learning explanations, though the study uses a small dataset and is not about magnetism.

30-year survey of crystal structure prediction finds no dominant method

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

This survey looks back over three decades of crystal structure prediction. In a 46-target leaderboard, the best template-based method has higher top-1 recovery than leading generative AI models, though the differences are not statistically significant against several of them. The authors also audit 68 experimentally examined materials, making the piece a useful reality check on how much to trust new AI structure claims.

Additive Manufacturing

Dual-loop policy-gradient control stabilizes LPBF surface temperature

Additive Manufacturing (journal) · 5/10

Laser powder bed fusion is a metal 3D printing process, and this paper uses a policy-gradient reinforcement learning controller to hold surface temperature steady. The abstract reports a simulation plus a physical LPBF validation, with controller tuning done offline from one uncontrolled calibration layer. The gain is modest: a 3.4% reduction in mean tracking error compared with a Bayesian-optimization baseline, and the temperature sensing serves control rather than defect detection.

GreenMelt computes part-scale melt pools in seconds with latent heat and Marangoni

Additive Manufacturing (journal) · 5/10

GreenMelt is a fast melt-pool model that includes latent heat and Marangoni flow, the surface-tension-driven motion of liquid metal. The abstract reports 1-10 second laptop runtimes against 3.5-5.5 hours for computational fluid dynamics, with under 3% mean relative error in the mushy zone on single tracks. Fast physics models like this could help train monitoring systems, but the validation shown is for single tracks, so agreement at full part scale is still to be confirmed.

Federated physics-informed neural operators predict thermal fields on unseen geometries

arXiv · ML for manufacturing · 5/10

Fed-PIGANO is a federated approach in which several sites train a shared physics-informed neural operator without pooling their raw data. The abstract reports 1.83-2.04% relative L2 error across 12 scenario-site cases, compared with up to 20.46% for local-only training. The benchmark is a 2D steady-state simulation, so it is a surrogate-model result rather than live sensing.

Cambridge Sensotec on in-machine oxygen sensing for consistent quality

3D Printing Industry · 4/10

A vendor interview describes a gas analyser that sits inside metal printers and measures oxygen at ppm levels, pitched as a route to consistent part quality. In-chamber oxygen sensing is a different signal from the melt-pool imaging that most monitoring work uses. The item is only a teaser, so its performance claims are unconfirmed.

Theoretical Physics

Foundation tensor networks locate the quantum glass transition via finite-size scaling

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 7/10

A neural network generates a tensor-network ground state directly from a Hamiltonian. The abstract reports critical parameters for the quantum Edwards-Anderson glass transition from finite-size scaling, averaged over 500,000 disorder realizations. It pairs machine learning with finite-size scaling, a standard way to locate critical points from small systems, but the model is quantum and disordered, so it does not transfer directly to classical Monte Carlo.

Holographic picture of the transverse-field Ising model predicts its stress from entanglement

arXiv · high-energy theory · 6/10

Holography proposes that the entanglement of a quantum system can be encoded as curved space. The authors reconstruct such a geometry for the transverse-field Ising model from its entanglement entropy, predict an energy-like stress, and compare it with the exact answer, which was not used in the reconstruction. The abstract reports close agreement in the near-critical regime, linking a textbook model to gravity-style ideas, though a field-theory derivation is still open.

Can gravity's quantum nature show up even when dephasing destroys entanglement?

arXiv · quantum physics · 6/10

One proposed test of quantum gravity has two masses become entangled through their gravitational interaction, but noise usually erases that entanglement. The authors prove that the gravitational phase evolution can still be distinguished from classical-noise models even when the state is separable, meaning unentangled. The result depends on the classical mediator models considered, so it is a proposal rather than a measurement.

Strong Mpemba effect demonstrated optically in a single qubit

Phys.org · Quantum physics · 6/10

The Mpemba effect is when a system starting farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one starting closer to it. According to the summary, an optical experiment demonstrates the strong version of the effect in a single qubit. Only the introduction of the press item is available, so the measurement details are unconfirmed.
